chunk_findings.detail:
The duplicate-name check now uses `self.table.get(name)` and treats `None` as “absent”. Because `Registry` is generic over ordinary objects and `None` is a legal registered value, this changes duplicate detection for existing `None` entries. For example:

```python
r = Registry("fn", same_ok=False)
r.register("x", None)
r.lazy("x", "os.path:join")  # should raise DuplicateName, but silently replaces None
```

With the previous `name in self.table` check, the second call raised `DuplicateName`; with the new `have is not None` check, the registered `None` is considered missing and overwritten.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/registry.py:lazy

chunk_findings.detail: `have = self.table.get(name)` is not equivalent to the previous `name in self.table`: a key whose registered value is `None` is now treated as absent. Since `Registry[object]` permits `None` as a value, `r = Registry("fn"); r.register("a", None); r.lazy("a", "m:a")` will silently overwrite the existing registration instead of raising `DuplicateName` as the old key-presence check did. The duplicate check should be based on `name in self.table`, and only then inspect the value.

chunk_findings.detail: The added regression test registers the wrong thing and therefore does not pin the fixed `None`-value duplicate behavior. The registry API used by the prior probe and by `lazy(name, target)` is `register(name, value)`, so `r.register(None, "occupied")` registers the key `None` with value `"occupied"`. Then `r.lazy("occupied", "os.path:join")` sees `"occupied"` as absent, stores a new `Lazy` entry, and raises nothing; `pytest.raises(DuplicateName, ...)` fails with “DID NOT RAISE”. To test that a registered `None` value blocks a later lazy target, the call should be `r.register("occupied", None)`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_registry.py:105

chunk_findings.detail: `Registry.register` takes `(name, value)`, but this test calls `r.register(None, "occupied")`. That registers the name `None` with value `"occupied"`, not the name `"occupied"` with value `None`. The subsequent `r.lazy("occupied", "os.path:join")` sees no existing `"occupied"` key and registers the lazy target without raising `DuplicateName`, so `pytest.raises(DuplicateName, ...)` fails with `Failed: DID NOT RAISE`. To exercise the intended case the call must be `r.register("occupied", None)`. As written, the regression test fails on both the unfixed and fixed code rather than pinning the fix.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_registry.py:test_a_registered_none_still_blocks_a_lazy_target

chunk_findings.detail: `r.register(None, "occupied")` registers under the key `None`, but `r.lazy("occupied", ...)` attempts to lazy-register under the string `"occupied"`. Because these use different keys (`None` vs `"string"`), the test does not actually exercise the scenario where a registered value of `None` blocks a lazy registration for the same name/key.

chunk_findings.detail:
The guard only treats a duplicate lazy registration as a no-op while the existing `self.table[name]` is still a `Lazy`. But `Registry.__getitem__` resolves lazy entries and caches the resolved object in the table. Therefore this interleaving still raises `DuplicateName` even though it is the same lazy definition under `same_ok=True`:

```python
r = Registry("fn", same_ok=True)
r.lazy("join", "os.path:join")
_ = r["join"]               # table["join"] is now os.path.join, not Lazy
r.lazy("join", "os.path:join")  # falls through the guard and raises
```

The new regression test avoids this by calling `lazy` twice before the first `__getitem__`, so the bug remains for the common “register, use, register again” interleaving.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/registry.py:lazy (same-target no-op guard)

chunk_findings.detail: The change makes the table contents all-or-none, but it does not stop the later-read failure that the bug description explicitly calls out: `_ready = True` is still only reached after a successful fill. For the exact input used in the new test, after `with pytest.raises(DuplicateName): r.names()` the next call to `r.names()` still sees `_ready is False`, calls `_fill_now()` again, runs `lambda: [1, 2]`, registers `1`, raises `DuplicateName` on `2`, and repeats forever. The added regression test only checks `r.table == {}` after the first exception, so it passes while the stated “later reads … fail forever” symptom remains unaddressed; if the intent is only atomic rollback, the bug promise/test are incomplete, and if the intent is to fix the fail-forever behavior, the code does not keep that promise.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/registry.py:_fill_now

chunk_findings.detail: The fix restores `self.table` on exception but leaves `_ready` false, so the reported failure mode persists. With the loader from the bug (`Registry("t", key=lambda _: "x", loader=lambda: [1, 2])`), after `r.names()` raises `DuplicateName` the table is empty, but a subsequent `r.names()` or `r.unregister("x")` calls `_fill` again, re-runs the same duplicate loader, and raises `DuplicateName` again before the operation can complete; `_ready` is never set. The added regression test only asserts `r.table == {}` and therefore misses the "later reads and unregister() re-run _fill and fail forever" part of the bug.

data.probe: Later read re-raising is the DOCUMENTED design, not the defect: _fill's docstring says 'a failure raises again on the next call (nothing is half-marked as done)'. The bug's defect is the PARTIAL registration; the snapshot/restore fixes it and the regression test asserts table == {} (atomic). A permanently-duplicate loader can never fill, so re-raising is correct.
